examples.title: Select a key
examples.note: A key selector is always double-quoted, so the query must be wrapped in single quotes in a shell.

examples.title: Walk down nested keys
examples.note: Selectors sit next to each other with no separator. Each one descends one level.

examples.title: Keys that need escaping
examples.note: A key carrying a quote or a backslash is written the way JSON writes it. The full escape set is supported: \" \\ \/ \b \f \n \r \t and \uXXXX.

examples.title: An empty key
examples.note: The empty string is a valid JSON key, so it is a valid selector.

examples.title: A key that does not exist
examples.note: The error names the key and shows the object it was looked for in.

examples.title: Select one index
examples.note: Indexes are zero-based.

examples.title: Select several indexes
examples.note: Indexes are returned in the order you ask for them, not in the order they appear.

examples.title: A range
examples.note: Ranges are inclusive at both ends.

examples.title: A reversed range
examples.note: Writing the bounds backwards reverses the result. There is no separate reverse operator.

examples.title: An open range
examples.note: Leave a bound out and it runs to the end. [:1] does the same from the start.

examples.title: The whole array
examples.note: Both bounds omitted selects everything, which is useful as the last step of a pipe.

examples.title: An index out of bounds
examples.note: The error reports the index and the array it was applied to.

examples.title: Several keys at once
examples.note: A multi key selector keeps the order you wrote, so it doubles as a way to reorder an object.

examples.title: Select keys by position
examples.note: An object index selector picks entries by position rather than by name.

examples.title: A range over positions
examples.note: Object ranges behave like array ranges, including the reversed and open forms.

examples.title: A reversed object range
examples.note: Same rule as arrays: bounds written backwards give a reversed result.

examples.title: Flatten nested arrays
examples.note: The flatten operator collapses every level of nesting into a single array.

examples.title: Flatten an object
examples.note: On an object, flatten joins the path with dots and keeps the leaf value.

examples.title: List the keys of an object
examples.note: The keys operator answers what is in here, which is the usual first move on an unfamiliar document. Keys come back sorted alphabetically, not in document order.

examples.title: List the indexes of an array
examples.note: On an array the same operator returns indexes rather than keys.

examples.title: Truncate to a primitive
examples.note: Truncate maps the output to a bare primitive, turning a big array into [] and an object into {}. Useful to check a shape without printing it.

examples.title: Truncate must come last
examples.note: Only one truncate operator is allowed and it has to be the final token.

examples.title: Apply a selector to every element
examples.note: The pipe in operator applies everything that follows to each element of an array, collecting the results.

examples.title: Pick several fields from every element
examples.note: Anything that works on one element works inside a pipe, including multi key selectors.

examples.title: Stop piping and select from the result
examples.note: The pipe out operator ends the iteration, so the tokens after it apply to the collected array as a whole.

examples.title: Reach into nested elements
examples.note: After a pipe out you can range, index or slice the collected array like any other array.

examples.title: Keep elements that have a key
examples.note: A lens with no value keeps every element where the selector resolves, regardless of what it holds.

examples.title: Filter on a value
examples.note: Give the lens a value and it keeps only the elements matching it. Values can be a boolean, null, a number or a string.

examples.title: Filter on a nested value
examples.note: A lens takes a whole path, not just one key.

examples.title: Several conditions
examples.note: Conditions separated by commas act as OR: an element is kept when any of them matches.

examples.title: Filter on a boolean
examples.note: Booleans and null are written bare, without quotes.

examples.title: Build an array from sub-queries
examples.note: A group separator runs each sub-query against the same input and collects the results into an array. Unlike a multi key selector it keeps no keys.

examples.title: Combine unrelated paths
examples.note: Each side of the comma is a full query, so groups reach into completely different parts of a document.

examples.title: Group whole pipelines
examples.note: Sub-queries may contain pipes, ranges, anything. The group is the outermost structure.

examples.title: Several documents at once
examples.note: Concatenated documents, with or without whitespace between them, are each evaluated and produce one result apiece.

examples.title: Documents separated by newlines
examples.note: Newline-delimited JSON works the same way, which is what most log pipelines produce.

examples.title: Inline the output
examples.note: Output is pretty-printed by default. Use -i or --inline for a single line, which is what you want when piping into another tool.

examples.title: Drop the quotes around a string
examples.note: With -r or --raw-string a string result is printed bare, so it can be assigned to a shell variable.

examples.title: Sort every object key
examples.note: -S or --sort-keys sorts keys recursively, matching jq's -S. Handy for diffing two documents.

examples.title: Check that input is valid JSON
examples.note: -v or --validate ignores the query and reports whether the input parses, setting the exit code accordingly.

examples.title: Filter, then project
examples.note: A lens narrows the array, then a pipe projects each survivor. This is the shape most real queries take.

examples.title: Filter on a nested value
examples.note: The lens path reaches into each element, so you can filter on something nested and still project from the top.

examples.title: Project several fields at once
examples.note: A multi key selector inside a pipe reshapes every element, which is how you trim a wide API response down to what you need.

examples.title: Filter, project, take the first
examples.note: Pipe out ends the iteration, so the index applies to the collected array rather than to each element.

examples.title: Slice the piped result
examples.note: Anything that works on an array works after a pipe out, including reversed ranges.

examples.title: Combine two unrelated pipelines
examples.note: A group separator runs each side against the same document, so a summary field and a filtered list arrive together in one array.

examples.title: Reach through a range into a pipe
examples.note: Select a slice first and the pipe applies only to it, which is cheaper than piping the whole array and slicing after.

examples.title: Keys of every element
examples.note: The keys operator inside a pipe reports the shape of each element. Useful when elements are not uniform.

examples.title: Flatten a nested selection
examples.note: Piping collects an array of arrays; flatten then collapses it into one flat list. Flatten only unnests arrays — objects inside an array are left whole.

examples.title: Filter on a number
examples.note: Lens values are not limited to strings. Here a number picks one element, and the projection keeps a nested object whole.

examples.title: Mix array and object addressing
examples.note: An array index picks the element, then an object range takes its first two entries by position. Selectors compose regardless of which kind of container they address.
